summary.text: Magma is the molten or semi-molten natural material, found beneath Earth's surface, from which all igneous rocks form.
It is made by melting of the mantle or crust in settings such as subduction zones, continental rifts, mid-ocean ridges and hotspots.
Its silica content tracks properties such as viscosity: silica-rich felsic magmas are extremely viscous, while basaltic magmas have relatively low viscosity.

facts.label: What it contains
facts.value: Molten rock, suspended crystals and gas bubbles

items.prompt: Very silica-rich magma rises to a volcano's vent. How is it most likely to erupt?

options.label: As long, fast rivers of runny lava
Explosively, blasting out fragments
As a gentle flow under the sea
As steam with no rock at all

items.explain: High silica makes felsic magma extremely viscous, so felsic lavas usually erupt explosively and produce fragmental deposits.

items.prompt: Four magmas differ in how much silica they contain. Which one would you expect to flow most easily?

options.label: The one with the most silica
The one with medium silica
Silica makes no difference
The one with the least silica

items.explain: Viscosity tracks silica content: felsic magmas are extremely viscous, while low-silica mafic and ultramafic magmas are far runnier.

items.prompt: Basalt lava flows a long way from its vent before it stops. What shape of volcano does it tend to build?

options.label: A broad, low shield volcano
A tall, steep-sided cone
A small, rounded lava dome
A deep crater with no rim

items.explain: Because runny basalt lava travels far from the vent, it tends to make low-profile shield volcanoes or flood basalts.

items.prompt: Komatiite lavas erupted on the ancient Earth, but none are known erupting today. Why not?

options.label: Volcanoes have all become extinct
The oceans now cover them all
Earth's mantle has cooled too much
The needed magnesium ran out

items.explain: No modern komatiites are known because the mantle has cooled too much to produce such highly magnesian magmas.

items.prompt: Magma rises toward the surface and the weight of rock pressing on it drops. What happens to the gases dissolved in it?

options.label: They come out of the liquid as bubbles
They sink to the bottom of the magma
They freeze into solid crystals
They dissolve in even more deeply

items.explain: As overburden pressure falls, dissolved gases bubble out, so magma near the surface holds solid, liquid and gas together.

items.prompt: Some magma never reaches a volcano and hardens deep underground instead. What does it form?

options.label: A lava flow on the ground
An intrusion such as a dike or sill
A layer of sandstone
A cloud of volcanic ash

items.explain: Magma that solidifies underground forms an intrusion, such as a dike, sill, laccolith, pluton or batholith.
